description_full: EACO Corporation, through its subsidiary, Bisco Industries, Inc., distributes and sells electronic components and fasteners in the United States, Asia, Canada, and internationally. The company offers electronic components, such as spacers and standoffs, card guides and ejectors, component holders and fuses, circuit board connectors, and cable components, as well as various fasteners and hardware products. It also offers customized services and solutions for various production needs, including special packaging, bin stocking, kitting and assembly, bar coding, electronic requisitioning, integrated supply programs, and others. In addition, the company's supplies parts used in the manufacture of products to a range of industries, such as aerospace, circuit board, communication, computer, fabrication, instrumentation, industrial equipment and marine sectors. EACO Corporation sells its products primarily to the original equipment manufacturers through its sales representatives and distribution centers. The company was founded in 1973 and is headquartered in Anaheim, California.

financial_summary: EACO Corp. is a small-cap technology business with a $729M market cap on $428M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and +12% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are contracting by -25.8pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 8% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 29%.

The business throws off $16M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.53×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.1× net debt/EBITDA.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 96% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

news_headlines.title: EACO GAAP EPS of $3.19, revenue of $163.9M (OTCMKTS:EACO)

sect: Its 10% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.42x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+13.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 66% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 53% and a beta of 0.46, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.62 vs 5y 0.16), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $38K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 46% in the 2020 crash, 16% in the 2022 bear market and 83% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 43% below its DCF fair value of $262, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 23%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $121 to $568 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Technology peers: cheaper on P/E 15.3 vs 26.7 and EV/EBITDA 10.5 vs 16.4, richer on P/FCF 45.9 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 147% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 11.4% annual cash-flow growth, 10pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 14pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It runs a 29% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9, but cash conversion of only 0.53x.
ROE of 21% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.1x net debt to EBITDA ($728K of cash against $4.2M of debt), with interest covered 205.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 9.8, in the safe zone).
The Beneish M-score (-2.07) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.5% over 3 years, 13.7% over 5 years and 11.8% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 22.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (0.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 95.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 0%.
